1:
Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) begins by separating the order of the book from the order of events. In both texts, he says, this story naturally follows the removal of the ark, although the events themselves appear to belong to a later period of David’s reign, when the Lord had given him rest round about from all his enemies; the promise about his seed indicates some time before the birth of Solomon, but the date cannot be more exactly determined. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) sets the chapter out as an argument instead, that David consults Nathan about building a temple, that God sends him an answer by Nathan informing him that Solomon shall build the house, and that David receives the divine purpose with humility and joy and gives God praise; for the detail of it he refers the reader to his notes on the parallel in Samuel.

Ellicott finds the chronicler’s hand in the choice of two words. Where this account names David three times in as many clauses, Samuel has simply the king — and the chronicler, he remarks, loves the name of his ideal sovereign. Where this account has God, Samuel has Jehovah, though the same verses had just said the ark of God. On the timing of Nathan’s correction he notes that the phrase the same night indicates a dream as the method of communication.

The refusal itself is worded quite differently in the two books. This account states it flatly, and Ellicott would render it more pointedly still, that it is not thou that shalt build me the house to dwell in; Samuel puts the same thing as a question implying its own denial, wilt thou build me a house for me to dwell in? And where this account says the house with the definite article, Ellicott explains it by the chronicler’s vantage point: he is thinking of the famous temple of Solomon, which by his day needed no further description.

On Nathan’s first and hastier answer, that David should do all that was in his heart, Ellicott pauses over the organ named. According to Hebrew ideas the heart was the seat of the mind and the will as well as of the emotions — a conception he thinks better than what passed for anatomy long after, since even Aristotle, seven centuries later than David, supposed the brain to be merely a kind of cooling counterpoise to the heat of the liver.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) leaves the collation aside and takes the opening for an example. It shows, he says, how desirous and solicitous good people should be to serve the interests of God’s kingdom in the world to the utmost of their capacity: David could not be easy in a house of cedar while the ark was lodged within curtains, for the concerns of the public should always be near our hearts, and what pleasure can we take in our own prosperity if we see not the good of Jerusalem? He presses the contrast with what a man newly advanced to wealth and power might have been expected to ask — not what he shall do for his children to get portions for them, nor what he shall do to fill his coffers and enlarge his dominions, but what he shall do for God.
7:
Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds the force of the opening in a pronoun and corrects a tense. The pronoun, he says, is emphatic — I it was who took thee from the pasture — and where this account says from following the sheep the Hebrew reads from behind, Samuel preserving the older form of the preposition. More consequentially, where the English has that God has made David a name like the name of the great men of the earth, Ellicott would render it rather as a promise still to come, and I will make thee; and he identifies those great men concretely as the sovereigns of Egypt and Babylon, of Tyre, and of the Hittite states. The cutting off of all David’s enemies he takes to refer not merely to the death of Saul and the overthrow of his house but to the successful conclusion of wars recorded in the chapters that follow.

What the promise of a settled place answers to is read two ways. Ellicott takes it of a tenure that had never yet been secure: although Israel had effected a settlement in Canaan, the history seems to show that down to the times of David the tribal boundaries were subject to great fluctuation, and the inroads of surrounding peoples made their hold very uncertain. He notes that the Hebrew keeps Israel singular throughout, him and he and his where the English has the plural, and glosses the phrase in their place as in his own stead or fixed habitation, comparing our own homestead and farmstead. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) refers the same promise much further back, taking the children of wickedness who shall waste them no more to mean that Israel shall never again be brought into servitude as they were when they sojourned in Egypt. Ellicott adds a complaint about the verse division, that the clause about the days of the judges ought never to have been separated from what precedes it, which it properly concludes.

On the way David is told he will die, two voices notice the same oddity and one goes further. Ellicott observes that the phrase runs literally to go with thy fathers, an unusual expression, where Samuel has the ordinary thou shalt lie down with thy fathers. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) agree that it is used of going the way of death and is similar to the phrase about going the way of all the world, but then make the sharper claim: this unusual form is the more primitive of the two, and Samuel’s familiar lying down with the fathers is the later and more usual idiom. Ellicott also judges the introductory phrase of the verse to be wanting in Samuel and probably to be supplied there from the Greek.

The promise of a throne for ever divides the collator from the expositor. Ellicott keeps to the comparison, noting that the pronoun is again the emphatic word, that where this account has build me an house Samuel has for my name, and that his throne stands here for Samuel’s throne of his kingdom, which he calls a characteristic abridgment. Clarke reads straight past the wording to the person, holding that David was a type of Christ and that concerning him the prophecy is literally true, with a prophet’s words about the increase of government and peace pointing the same way; of the mercy that shall not be taken away he says plainly that God will not cut off this family from the throne as he cut off that of Saul before him. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) answers a question the others do not raise, whether David must think his purpose vain and the reward of it lost: no, for it being God’s own act that prevented the execution, he shall be as fully recompensed as if the thing had been done.
16:
Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) announces his method before using it. The prayer, he says, was largely observed on the parallel in Samuel, so that here he will note only those few expressions in which this record differs from that one and has something added to it. The difference he fastens on is a change of mood: what stands there as a question, whether this is the manner of men, appears here as an acknowledgment, that God has regarded David according to the estate of a man of high degree — God having made him a great man and then treated him accordingly. Of the prayer as a whole he observes how humbly David abases himself and acknowledges his own unworthiness, how highly he advances the name of God and admires his condescending grace, with what devout affections he magnifies the God of Israel and with what assurance he builds upon the promise and puts it in suit. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reproduces that last passage almost word for word, down to the closing petition that the Lord would enable us all thus to seek him.

Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) works the same clause as Henry but from the Hebrew, and finds it simply obscure, noting that Samuel has the plainer and shorter reading, that this is the law of man, and that the word for law has been supposed to mean manner or custom in this place. On the opening question he observes that Samuel uses the longer form of the pronoun where this account has the shorter, and that where this account addresses God as Jehovah Elohim, Samuel has the form meaning my Lord Jehovah, which he judges the more original of the two. He draws out the courtesy of that address: David calls God my Lord just as God in the earlier verses had called David my servant, and he compares the frequent style of the Assyrian kings, who speak of their wars as undertaken in the service of the gods their lords. The sitting before the Lord he places in the tent of the ark.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) answers the question of the prayer in a single line of self-abasement, that David asks what his house is because he is not of any regal family and has no natural right at all to the throne.

At the next verse Ellicott proposes two emendations and is candid that they are emendations. Samuel, he notes, has the word for speak which this account omits; and the word here translated for the honour may itself be a corruption of that very word, so that the question would run, what can David speak more to thee. In the same verse the phrase of thy servant stands in the accusative and should in his judgment be struck out altogether as a mistaken repetition of the same word at the end of the verse. Neither change is offered as certain, and both are proposed on the ground that the Hebrew as it stands reads awkwardly beside the older text.
20:
Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) distinguishes two words the English blurs. Where the question runs what one nation in the earth is like thy people Israel, he would render it who is like thy people Israel, a single and isolated race upon the earth; and he separates the terms behind it, one meaning a race, a people considered as united by common blood and speech and country, the other a political community or state owning one sovereign. In the same verse he records a variant of some weight: where this account says which God went to redeem to himself as a people, Samuel has the plural, which gods went — so that the chronicler’s text reads as a correction of the older one. The making of a name he takes to mean for God himself.

Twice he suspects the Chronicles text of damage or of expansion. At the verse about God’s giving Israel to himself for a people, where Samuel has a verb meaning confirmed it, he judges that our reading is probably the result of partial obliteration. At the next petition he notes that the doubled let it even be established is wanting in Samuel altogether, and then observes something that changes the sense: the words let be are not in the Hebrew, so that the clause about the house of David may not be a petition at all but part of what men are to say hereafter in praise of God — the house of David thy servant is established before thee.

On a phrase he calls unique in Hebrew the two voices gloss differently. Ellicott renders that David hath found his heart, which he explains as having taken courage, the noun being expressed in Samuel and omitted here; and he gives the preceding clause literally as God having uncovered the ear of his servant, where Samuel has the more usual form, saying, a house I will build thee. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) takes it from the Targum instead, which he thinks expresses the full sense: therefore thy servant hath found an opening of mouth, that he might pray before thee.

The closing verses show the chronicler turning request into accomplished fact, which is the same movement noticed earlier in the prayer. Ellicott would render the last petition not as a request that it may please God to bless but as a statement that he has willed to bless, where Samuel has plainly be willing, and bless; and for thou blessest he reads for thou hast blessed, remarking that Samuel is as usual the fuller of the two. He notes too that the chronicler drops the clause which follows in Samuel, that God’s words become truth. Clarke again prefers the Targum’s expansion, that God begins to bless the house of his servant and therefore it shall be blessed for ever; and he states his own practice outright, asking the reader to refer to his notes on the parallel in Samuel for the many particulars belonging to these places, which he says it would answer no good purpose to repeat here. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) closes on the title itself, that God is really to his people what he has styled himself, their God, having taken such care of them and shown such mercy and truth as fully answered that name.
